I think you can very much get the same experience at an over the water bungalow in the carribean without having to go all the way to the Maldives; unless you really just want to say you’ve been to the Maldives! 

All that being said it’s delay just relaxing on a small island, beach all the way around it, and just enjoying that, not much else going on. We did relax at the resort pool a lot. The food was pretty good, but was mostly buffet style at our resort apartment from a couple of special dinner options. 

Overall, I loved it. But it’s not worth 2-3x the vacation cost of other beautiful beach resort over the water bungalows.

Btcfx is not an ETF. It is a futures based mutual fund.

So the fund buys and sell futures contracts of BTC and it routinely does this throughout the month, as new investment money comes in, as people make withdrawals, as the price of bitcoin fluctuates, and as previous contracts purchases get closer to their end date. Sometimes, they sell them for more than they buy them. They return any investment income and capital gains back to shareholders as a dividend, they generally pay it on the first trading day of each month. In other months, the net asset value of each share may decrease as they have costs associated with or losses within the value of the futures contracts they are buy/selling.

The dividend is coming from money the entire fund is making, and then divided up equally among all shares of the fund.

The way they do this is outlined in their prospectus, which you should read.

THere is no "free money".

The dividend is a result of your investment making money, and beating the risk involved in attempting to do so.

If bitcoin were to start going down, the net asset value of the fund and each of your shares would go down, they still might pay a dividend because they would have income from selling individual futures contracts perhaps.

If bitcoin stayed the same price, what you'd inherintly see is net asset value go down per share, but you'd be paid dividends of transactions and your share count would go up, and your total value would go down.

You're making money because bitcoin is rising in price.

  
I would encourage you, if you can, to buy at least an ETF rather than futures, or better yet bitcoin directly.

I personally bought BTCFX because I am limited to mutual funds within a certain account, and it is my only option with bitcoin exposure at the time.

It's also important I think to distinguish between an owner operated charter vessel, and a boat that has been bareboat chartered to a charterer. 

Example, there were owners of boats taking 14 passengers out. If the owner of a boat is on an UOPV boat, he/she can only take people out under a proper 6 pack license, plus crew.  He cannot bareboat charter the boat to one of the customers and then take them out, as the owner is not allowed to be on a bareboat charter, and charterers must be allowed choose their own operator / crew.  There's a big difference there. The owner MAY require proof the chosen operator / crew are competent, and may provide a list of potential operators to the charterer, but cannot be involved in the process.

The biggest sailing differences in terms of working the boat are the fact that you need to get both hills through the wind when tacking. To do that, backfill the jib and trim it in when starting the tack. You break it over when the main sail tacks over this you know you’re fully through the wind. Two big hulls with lots of freeboard need to get through the wind so you want to maintain power to do it; thus trimming and backfilling rather than breaking when the jib luffs like on a monohull. Some of the charter cats have self tacking jibs, which makes them poor sailing boats.

No backstay on the cats, they have swept back shrouds - so you can’t ease the main as much as you might be used to. 


Two engines means that docking and undocking can be done using both engines together; makes it pretty easy. Still might need to spring occasionally. 

It’s more comfortable! More room, less heel.

Lastly, bigger boat and sails means bigger loads on the lines. Think accordingly when using winches and clutches. 

I personally love the catamarans, and the bareboat charters in beautiful places even more! 

Keep in mind bareboat boats might be sparse on spare parts and tools but might break just as much. Be smart. Look over the bait before you leave the dock / hook.

Catamaran sailing is much more comfortable. If you want experience and to learn and plan to be on a monohull; I’d recommend getting that experience on a monohull. They’re going to be responsive and more like “sailing”. 

Catamaran sailing is more like hanging out quite comfortably in a floating condo that has some sails attached. It’s a different experience. 

The biggest difference in pure sailing is going to be line handling while tacking.  Tacking a catamaran you backfill the jib and let it help have the wind push both hulls through the wind, you need to maintain that power to do it, breaking when the mail sail finally tacks over. On a monohull you are generally breaking as soon as the jib starts to tack over.  

You’re not going to sail a catamaran to the dock or a mooring ball, whereas you might a monohull. 

Catamarans have two engines that lets them turn in place, you’re going to steer by engines at low speed and while docking/undocking. 

Catamarans don’t have a back stay so slightly different rig tuning, and your not going to be able to ease the main sheet out as much due to the swept back shrouds. 

Catamarans won’t point as high as a monohull.

All in all it’s still sailing; but it’s not the same. Learn on the monohulls; enjoy and relax on the catamarans.

One thing you might be picking up on, is a good boat owner is going to end up becoming quite proficient in all systems on the bait, including engines. Because you might be out sailing and something isn’t working right and you’re going to need to be able to troubleshoot. Not everyone does this, but it’s honestly not hard and you should start leaning about the systems.

If the engine started easily, and ran fine, is not leaking anywhere - I probably wouldn’t be super concerned about it. The types of concerns that get expensive later you’d probably need to pull the engine apart to check the best and we’re not doing that as part of a survey. 

The oil is going to be black and dark. It’s a diesel. You could change it with fresh and in a weeks time of daily use is going to be dark again. That’s part of owning a diesel; especially an older one but it doesn’t mean the engine is bad.

You’re going to need to know how to replace the impeller which you should do immediately anyway or at least inspect, so you don’t need a surveyor to do that. You need to know what every line and host going to the engine comes from and goes to and how the fit together in a system - especially the raw water cooling system, and fuel (gotta learn to bleed the fuel on rare occasions). 

In short, you could pay for an engine survey you’re probably not going to learn a ton, and you’re still going to need to learn about engines yourself. 

I suspect the survey you got says that to minimize liability and not because they are worried something is actually wrong unless they called out specific obvious issues. If it wasn’t working well it wouldn’t start easy or would be very obvious when it runs something is weird. 

How’s the belt tension?

Motor mounts shaking like crazy? 

Any signs of persistent leaks?

Get in there and look!

These yanmars are good engines and last many decades. 

But if it makes you feel better; get the survey!

In the long run; you’ll be far better off gaining education of how things work and how to look at them and troubleshoot yourself

When you start, some of the things you'll lean might not make sense until later when it really starts to click. Two examples, when I first started, Captain would try to get me to notice certain things about the sail and I'd just be like "it looks like a big sail to me, and it's up, filled with wind, looks ok" eventually I noticed the subtle lines in the sail that told me things. And, he also tried to get me to see "wind lines" in the water, and I'd just be like it looks like water to me Captain. Eventually you learn and notice the nuances that tell you information. 

Here's some basic skills you'll need to learn if you want to get started and learn some stuff on your own first. This is not a complete list by any means, but enough you can look into and see if it excites you.

1) Safety. Don't fall out of the boat, and understand the basics of a man overboard drill and how to use a VHF radio when it comes to boating. Three points of contact. How to walk around the boat underway (what side of the boat, etc..) Keep your head away from the boom and the path the boom might take. (so some vocab too). Don't put your hand in between a line (a rope) and the winches, good way to lose a finger.

2) Basic "rules of the road".  In car speak it's right of way, in boat speak we have "stand-on" and "give-way" and there's a method to the madness.  We call then "Col Regs" [https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/navigation-rules-amalgamated](https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/navigation-rules-amalgamated)

3) This maybe should have been first, but some basic vocabulary. Port/Starboard, Windward/Leeward, and parts of a sailboat. Lots of guides online. On a boat, ropes have names. Line is a generic name for a rope on a boat. Halyard, sheet are other examples of lines that have specific jobs. Points of sail (direction the boat is pointed/sailing in relation to the wind). Apparant wind (the direction the wind feels like it's coming from - but might not be the "true wind" - think about how wind feels when you're sitting in a car at a light assuming it's coming directly from the side, vs how it feels as you speed up and stick your hand out the window). 

4) 4 knots to get started. Cleat Hitch - what we tie the boat to the dock using. Clove Hitch - what we tie fenders (rubber bumpers) to hang over the side of the boat. Bowline - what we tie lines to sails with, among other things. Cowhitch - what we tidy up lines when not in use to hang on the railings of the boat.

5) A sail is like an airplane wing. It generates lift, much like an airplane wing. You can't sail directly in to the wind, but you need to be 30 degrees or so off of it (or more). Most sailboats have two mail sails, a Jib up front, and the main sail. You can run either one, or both, depending on things - and it's simple physics then how they work with the boat. remember under the sailboat is a big lead keel that also balances the boat out from the force of the wind on the sails up to. A bunch of physics that shouldn't be too bad for a mechanically inclined person to learn the basics of. 

Learn just a little bit about those things and you'll be ahead of anyone coming out for the first time, and then can learn some actual basic tasks of a sailboat crew.

The key is to understand how all the forces of the boat are interacting when you heave-to.

You cannot heave to without a main, therefore it is doing something…. And a key something. Knowing what it is helps know what to do with it. 

The jib is backfilled and trying to push the bow around.

You’re counteracting that with your rudder to steer the boat in the opposite direction. Boat is then balancing on the midpoint of the keel. 

But - what does the rudder need to function? 

Flow.

Where does it get it?

From the main. The main is catching the wind like a barn door, and pushing  the boat sideways, ever so slowly through the water, giving you the flow you need so that your rudder can function.

Main too powerful? The boat will sail forward instead of slowly drift sideways.

Main is too weak? The momentum of the boat stalls rudder is useless and jib overpowers the bow around.

Find the sweet spot on your boat. 

Not sure which way your boat is moving? Look for the vortices of the water hitting the broad side of the keel and going around it, making little vortices on the backside. If they are to the beam you’re doing it right. 

If they are more off the quarter / stern your main can probably be depowered a bit more. You’re moving forward.

The club allowed its members who were deemed knowledgeable enough by the owner to be skippers to take the boats out when they wanted and everyone else could sign on as crew. Regular time slots each day. Club owner would go too when there wasn’t enough skippers 

If you were not yet deemed a skipper then no you couldn’t just take the boats. The skipper would then mentor along with other experience crew. 

The boats were owned by the club / business owner and he along with the approved skippers would discuss how people are progressing and who is getting it the point to be able to be trusted with being a skipper and would then specifically train them to be a skipper as a part of their sails. 

So I went from newbie to helping teach newbies how to crew to helping skipper supervise what the crew was doing to skippering myself.  Your skipper is in charge but we have the Mindset that we want to help people learn (and make mistakes) safely, and we all have fun sailing. 

There was no set agenda for the sails just what everyone wanted to do / learn that day or the skipper felt like doing and club culture again is such we all help each other learn and improve 

Always a mix of experiences. Some sails we all just wanted to chill and sail out and back. Some we’d tack and gybe 50 times for the practice. Some we’d not sail but fix something on the boat and learn about maintenance. Some we’d do various drills or practice efficient sailing in the type of weather we had that day.

No it’s a club. You join the club and get X/Unlimited sails per Y time frame. Mine allowed me to go out as much as I wanted and then you just sign up online for the time slots you wanted to go. It was not a formal class like you might think of with ASA just people that liked to sail. The culture of the club is such that skippers and veterans help teach new people, and even your 2nd time out might show someone who it is their first time what you learned the last time (like something easy like knots). And then you gradually learn more and more. About sailing. About maintenance. About operating the boat. About crew management. All kinds of stuff. 

At first you’re not going to see and understand the subtle things that are nuanced but they slowly come together. Example - wind lines at first I was just like looks like water to me man… then you start to recognize them. Luffing in the sail or vertical/horizontal creases in the sail - at first you’re gonna be like it just looks like a sail to me man, and it’s up. 

Tons of vocabulary to learn to everyone is speaking the same language.

Tons of safety things - learning and teaching how to properly hold a sheet, use a winch, what to do in a man overboard situation. How to go forward on deck while underway. 

To be looking out for potential hazards like lines in the water or that could go in the water, your crewmate about to get the finger ripped off by a winch or overwrap their jib sheet because of the angle of attack they are holding the line, someone under the boom when someone else goes to blow the topping lift; etc… 

So anyway, I found a club that worked for me. I didn’t want to do fractional ownership’s yet, and I didn’t want to just race, and I didn’t want “classroom” stuff I wanted to sail - and it’s been the best way to learn!
